title: Review: Wave model; Wave phenomena
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: C.2#c16 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; C.2.4#xt3 term and clue written for the game; C.3#c02 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C.3#c04 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: C.2#q10, C.2#q11, C.2#q15, C.3#q25, C.3#q26, C.3#q03, C.3#q05, C.2#q08, C.2#q13, C.2#q14, C.3#q01, C.3#q02. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Mechanical wave
items.clue: An oscillation of the particles of a material medium, such as sound.

items.label: Infrared
items.clue: The spectral region with wavelengths just longer than those of visible light.

items.label: Ray
items.clue: A line drawn to show the direction in which a wave, and the energy it carries, travels.

items.label: Reflection
items.clue: The change in direction of a wave at a boundary so that it returns into the medium it came from.

questions.stem: A student at one end of a long steel railway track puts an ear to the rail. At the other end, 1.0 km away, the rail is struck once with a hammer. The student hears two separate sounds, 0.20 s and 2.9 s after the blow. Which conclusion do these observations support?

options.text: Sound is slowed by closely packed particles: the first sound came through the air.
Sound has one fixed speed, so the second sound was an echo of the first sound.
Sound travels faster in steel than in air: the first sound came through the rail.
The blow pushed steel along the rail to the ear, so the sound through the rail came first.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the nature of electromagnetic waves?

options.text: Oscillations of the particles of the medium they travel through, so they cannot cross a vacuum
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel faster in a vacuum the higher their frequency
Streams of tiny charged particles given out by the source, which can travel through a vacuum
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel

questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves are transverse oscillations of electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. They need no medium and travel through a vacuum at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a difference between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves?

options.text: Mechanical waves are longitudinal waves, whereas electromagnetic waves are transverse.
Mechanical waves need a material medium; electromagnetic waves can also travel through a vacuum.
Mechanical waves change speed between media; electromagnetic waves keep speed c in all.
Mechanical waves transfer matter from place to place, whereas electromagnetic waves transfer energy.

questions.explanation: A mechanical wave is an oscillation of particles of a medium, so it needs one. An electromagnetic wave is an oscillation of electric and magnetic fields and travels through a vacuum as well as through many materials.

questions.stem: A small loudspeaker in open air emits sound of frequency 170 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. A student draws a wavefront–ray diagram of the sound in a horizontal plane through the speaker. Which statement about the diagram is correct?

options.text: Every compression and every rarefaction has a wavefront, so neighbouring ones are 1.0 m apart.
The rays show the paths along which air is carried outward from the speaker.
Adjacent wavefronts are 2.0 m apart, both close to the speaker and far from it.
There is no sound in the gaps between the rays that are drawn on the diagram.

questions.stem: Straight water waves of frequency 5.0 Hz travel at 0.40 m s⁻¹ across the deep part of a ripple tank towards a boundary with a shallow region, in which the wave speed is 0.20 m s⁻¹. The wavefronts are parallel to the boundary. Which statement about the waves at the boundary is correct?

options.text: The reflected waves have a wavelength of 8.0 cm and the transmitted waves 4.0 cm.
The transmitted waves have a wavelength of 8.0 cm, the same as that of the incident waves.
The transmitted waves have a frequency of 2.5 Hz, half that of the incident waves.
No waves are reflected at the boundary; all of the wave energy passes into the shallow water.

questions.stem: A person standing behind a tree trunk about 1 m wide can clearly hear a street musician on the other side of the trunk but cannot see her. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: Sound wavelengths, roughly 0.1 m to 3 m, are comparable with the trunk's width; light's are far smaller.
Light travels only in straight lines and cannot diffract; only mechanical waves bend round obstacles.
Sound and light diffract equally round the same trunk, but the diffracted light is too dim to see.
Sound diffracts round the trunk only because one of its wavelengths is exactly equal to the trunk's width.

questions.stem: On a wavefront diagram, straight wavefronts in deep water make an angle of 40° with the straight boundary of a region of shallow water. The wave speed in the shallow water is 0.75 times the wave speed in the deep water. What angle do the wavefronts in the shallow water make with the boundary?
Which statement describes the nature of a sound wave travelling through air?

options.text: A transverse wave in which air particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
A flow of air particles from the source to the ear, carrying the energy along with them
A longitudinal wave that, like light, can travel through a vacuum as well as through air
A longitudinal wave in which air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer

questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave. Air particles oscillate back and forth along the direction of travel about fixed positions, forming compressions and rarefactions (pressure variations) that travel outward.

questions.stem: In a vacuum, the radio waves from an FM radio station have a wavelength of 3.0 m, and the X-rays used in medical imaging have a wavelength of about 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. How do their frequencies compare?

options.text: The X-ray frequency is 3 × 10¹⁰ times the radio frequency, since f = c/λ.
The radio frequency is 3 × 10¹⁰ times the X-ray frequency, since f rises with λ.
The X-ray frequency is higher, because X-rays travel faster than radio waves.
They are equal, because both waves travel at the same speed, c, in a vacuum.

questions.explanation: Both travel at c in a vacuum, so f = c/λ and the ratio of frequencies is the inverse ratio of wavelengths: 3.0 m ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 3 × 10¹⁰. (f_radio = 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz, f_X-ray = 3.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz.)

questions.stem: An electric bell rings inside a sealed glass jar and can be both seen and heard. A pump gradually removes the air from the jar while the bell keeps working. Which prediction, with its explanation, is correct?

options.text: The sound fades and the bell vanishes from view, since both waves need air to travel.
Neither changes, because sound, like light, can travel through an evacuated jar.
The sound fades but the bell stays visible: light, unlike sound, needs no medium.
The sound fades but the bell stays visible, since only longitudinal waves need a medium.

questions.stem: Circular ripples spread out across a ripple tank from a vibrating dipper. A student sketches a wavefront–ray diagram of the waves. Which statement correctly describes the rays on the diagram?

options.text: They are drawn along the crests, parallel to the wavefronts, joining points that are in phase.
They trace the paths along which water moves outwards from the dipper as the wave travels.
They are thin beams that make up the wave, so there is no wave between two drawn rays.
They are perpendicular to the wavefronts and show the direction in which the wave's energy travels.

questions.stem: A narrow beam of monochromatic light in air strikes the flat surface of a glass block along the normal, so that the angle of incidence is 0°. Which statement about what happens at the surface is correct?

options.text: None of the light is reflected; it all passes into the glass.
The light entering the glass changes direction as it is refracted.
The light entering the glass keeps the frequency it had in air.
The light entering the glass keeps the wavelength it had in air.

questions.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source and does not change at a boundary. The light slows down in glass, so its wavelength decreases (λ = v/f); arriving along the normal, it does not change direction, and a few per cent of it is reflected back along the normal.
